Raise your hand…

Opening question for the audience. Play along.

Now keep it up if you know who invented it.

Exactly. Nobody does. Even historians argue about it.

Picture a Lebanese table: hummus, tabbouleh, olives, bread, kibbeh, pickles, grilled meat, sweets. Behind every plate is a question: where did it come from? And how did it become part of our culture? The answer isn’t one person, one empire or one country. It’s all of these on one table:

🌾 agriculture⛵ trade🧳 migration🕌 religion🏛️ empires

Today, we treat Lebanese food as a historical document.

The Tasting Game

Volunteers taste, guess where it comes from, the audience shouts hints. Answer to unlock the next one.

What makes it special?

Lebanese cuisine belongs to the Levantine and Eastern Mediterranean tradition. The principle is simple: sophisticated food from seasonal, local ingredients.

But it’s also about how and why we eat. Meals are shared. Guests are always offered food. Special dishes mark religious occasions; sweets mark births, weddings and holidays. Food becomes a form of communication.

A Lebanese person doesn’t just say “Welcome.”

Sometimes they say it by putting another plate on the table.

The Time Machine

Keep scrolling. Six layers of one cuisine appear one after another.

The Lebanese Mezze

If history explains where the food came from, mezze explains how we experience it together. Tap a dish.

Mezze isn’t a list of recipes. It’s a social architecture of food: everyone shares the table, reaches toward the same dishes and joins the same meal.

Karam · كرم

Generosity. Offering is itself the welcome.

Mouneh: saving the harvest

Dry, salt, ferment, pickle, preserve in oil. Click a jar to fill it.

Choose a jar from the shelf. Each one tells a story of surviving the winter.

1915 – 1918

Famine in Mount Lebanon: wartime blockades, requisitions, crop failures, locusts and transport problems. Mouneh existed before, but the famine reinforced it. Mouneh was a food-security system, and preserving food also means preserving knowledge.

In the glass

Continuity and change: even our drinks tell a story of globalization.

Edible markers of time

Nuts, dairy, semolina, pastry, syrup and floral aromas. You can tell what people celebrate by what appears on the dessert table.

Food helps create the celebration

Religious diversity, different traditions, one shared role for food.
